<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-grounded cases, but A's causal story (variable-reward mechanics, zero-sum attention economics) was more concrete and better withstood scrutiny than B's abstract vagueness/market-discipline defense. The decisive exchange was A's pressure question forcing B to answer whether a platform with clear internal proof of degraded outcomes and rising distrust owes any obligation to change — B answered "No," and A's closing correctly exploited that explicit concession as effectively negating B's own case, since B's later attempt to reframe it as "no clean trigger" rather than "no duty" came only after the fact and didn't erase the direct record. A also more convincingly rebutted B's "just switch apps" market-discipline argument by pointing out (a) same-parent-company competition is often illusory and (b) users cannot detect algorithmic suppression, making exit blind rather than corrective — a point B's closing conceded operates "at a different resolution" without fully resolving the detection problem. B's litigation-cost and vagueness arguments remained live and were never fully dissolved, keeping this competitive, but A controlled the framing and pressure-question exchange more decisively.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question in Turn 5 (Q1) forcing a direct yes/no on platform obligation, and B's explicit "No" answer in Turn 8 (A1), which A's closing then used to argue the motion had effectively been conceded.</best_rebuttal>
